gap: B's markers are louder and it drops the quote rule: #, ##, > render at #7A7A7A (~4.2:1 on the #F9F9F9 page) against A's #9E9E9E (~2.6:1) — roughly 40% darker ink on the scaffolding, so the hash marks pull the eye more than they should. B also has no blockquote left rule (A draws a ~2px #BFBFBF bar), and since B's quote text sits in exactly the same column as body prose, the quoted paragraph is flagged only by one hanging '>' and reads as an ordinary paragraph at a glance.
gapTheirs: A's prose column will not hold still: the markers live inside the text column, so the text left edge moves from x=673 (paragraph) to 721 (# heading), 744 (## heading), 722 (bullet), 747 (ordered item) — up to 74 device px / ~37 CSS px / ~3 monospace characters of horizontal jitter between block types. Worse, inside a single blockquote the first line's text starts at 721 but its wrapped line falls back to 676 — a 45px break mid-sentence, i.e. no hanging indent at all. B holds every text line at 672-675 and hangs all markers in a gutter right-aligned to x≈648 with a constant ~25px gap.
verdict: Same font, same 72px line rhythm, same 28px caps — the only real argument here is where the markers live, and A gets it backwards. In A, typing '## ' at the head of a line shunts the whole line right by 71px, and A's own blockquote can't keep its two lines in the same column, which is the exact stutter a writer feels when re-reading a draft. B pays for its clean flush-left column with markers that are a stop too dark and a quote block you have to hunt for; that is a colour-value fix, whereas A's is a layout model. And A's 6px cyan #00B5FF caret parks on top of the comma it precedes — B's 4px #1C1C1C caret at least doesn't eat punctuation.

states.name: dark
states.gap: No blockquote rule. A draws a 4px vertical bar at x=644 (#494949) spanning the full height of the quote; B marks the quote with a single 15px-wide grey '>' on line one only. From the wrap line onward B's quote is typographically indistinguishable from prose — both sit at x=673-674 in the same #1c1c1c at the same 72px pitch — so a six-line quote would lose its block identity entirely after the first line.
states.gapTheirs: Markers live in the text column, not a gutter: '#' sits at x=673 — the exact x of body prose — so heading text starts at 721, '##' heading text at 744, ordered-list text at 747, bullets/quote text at 721, while paragraphs start at 673. That is four different left edges spanning 74px (~2.5 monospace characters) down one column, and typing '# ' at line start physically shoves that line's text 48px right. Worst case is inside a single blockquote: line one's text is at 721, its own wrap line snaps back to 676 — a 45px break within one quote. B holds every text edge at 672-675 (max deviation 3px) and hangs markers into a right-aligned gutter ('#' and '##' both terminating at x=646, '-' at 641, '1.' at 637, constant ~28px gap to text).
states.verdict: B wins on one thing that outweighs everything else here: it has a left margin, and A does not. In A the text edge zigzags across 673/721/744/747 depending on block type, so scanning the page your eye tracks a 74px stagger instead of a line, and prefixing a paragraph with '#' kicks the text 48px sideways as you type — the exact jump this piece is supposed to prevent. A's own blockquote proves the model is broken: first line at 721, wrap line at 676, ragged inside a single quote. B's sin is narrower but real — it deletes the quote rule, so past line one a quote is pixel-identical to prose.
